# Interactive Tables {#chp:interactive}

A static table answers the question you thought to ask. An interactive table
lets your reader ask the ones you did not. Which cars have the most horsepower
per cylinder? Which species sits in the middle of the sepal lengths? Click a
header, type a phrase, drag a slider, and the answer is already on the screen.

The best part is the price. Everything interactive is handled in the browser by
an extension that loads only for tables that ask for it. Add
`lt_interactive()` to one table on a page and that page pulls in the extension;
leave it off and the table costs nothing extra.

```{r}
library(lt)
lt(mtcars[, 1:4]) |> lt_interactive()
```

Click a header to sort, use the box above the table to search, and page through
the rows with the controls below. Each feature is an option of `lt_interactive()`,
and each option can be switched off with `FALSE`, so you only ever pay for the
controls you keep.

## Searching and sorting {#sec:search-sort}

Let's start with the feature readers reach for first. This example combines
sorting and search, with the pager limited to five rows:

```{r, child = ex('sort-search')}
```

### Sorting {#sec:sort}

Click a column header once to sort ascending, again for descending, and a third
time to go back to the original order. Sorting uses the raw values, so numbers
sort as numbers (10 comes after 9, not after 1), and dates sort in time order
rather than alphabetically.

When one sort is not enough, shift-click a second header. The table then sorts
by the first column and breaks ties with the second, and each header shows its
place in the order.

You can also start the table already sorted. Give `sort` a character vector of
column names, where a `-` prefix means descending, or a one-sided formula with
the same rule (`~ cyl + -mpg`, for instance):

```{r}
lt(mtcars[, 1:4]) |> lt_interactive(sort = c("cyl", "-mpg"), search = FALSE, filter = FALSE, pager = 5)
```

### Search and the plain-language box {#sec:search}

The search box looks for a term in every cell of every row, and keeps only the
rows that match. Matching ignores case, so `merc` finds the Mercedes rows.

Typing a term is only the beginning. The box also reads a small, forgiving
mini-language that feels a lot like English. A condition names a column (by its
name, or by its label if the label has spaces), says what to check, and gives a
value:

```{r}
lt(mtcars[, 1:5]) |> lt_interactive(search = TRUE, pager = 5, filter = FALSE)
```

@tab:query-phrases shows the phrases the box understands, each with what it keeps.

:::: {.table #tab:query-phrases}
::: caption
[ ](#@tab:query-phrases) Phrases the search box understands.
:::

| You type | It keeps the rows where |
|:---------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| `mpg over 25` | `mpg` is greater than 25 (also `above`, `more than`) |
| `hp under 100` | `hp` is less than 100 (also `below`, `less than`) |
| `wt at least 3` | `wt` is 3 or more (`at most` is the other way round) |
| `mpg between 15 and 20` | `mpg` is from 15 to 20, inclusive |
| `cyl is 4` | `cyl` equals 4 (also `equals`) |
| `cyl is not 4` | `cyl` is anything but 4 |
| `cyl 6` | `cyl` contains `6`, in short form |
| `cyl contains 6` | the same, spelled out |
| `does not contain merc` | no cell mentions `merc` (also `excludes`) |
| `cyl is 4, mpg over 25` | both conditions hold (`,`, `;`, or `and` all work) |
| `cyl is 4 or cyl is 6` | either one holds (`or` gives alternatives) |
| `cyl is 4 or cyl is 6, mpg over 20` | `cyl` is 4, or `cyl` is 6 *and* `mpg` is over 20 |
| `"Hornet Sportabout"` | the quoted phrase, matched as one piece |
::::

Two rules make the mini-language predictable. First, `and` binds tighter than
`or`, so the last example reads as "4, or (6 and over 20)": the comma and `and`
group first, then `or` splits the alternatives. Second, any words that do not
form a condition are searched as typed, so `hornet` still does what you would
expect.

A line under the box shows how the query was read. If it reads `cyl is 4 or
cyl is 6` as you meant it, you are good to go; if it reads it differently, you
have found a typo before the rows have a chance to mislead anyone.

Click the box to see a few random queries built from the table's own values, and
pick one to run it. It is the fastest way to learn the mini-language, and it
works on any table, including tables you did not build yourself.

If the mini-language is too gentle for you, a term that mentions `x` is
evaluated as a JavaScript expression against each raw cell value. So `x > 20`
keeps every row where any cell is above 20, and `x == null` finds the missing
values. This is the power-user door, and it is open even when the friendly
phrases are not enough.

::: {.callout-warning data-legend="Expressions are JavaScript here"}
The `x` expression runs in the browser, so it speaks JavaScript, not R. Write
`x == 4`, not `x == 4L`, and `x >= "2024-01-05"` for dates. The same
expressions must be valid R if you serve the table from R (see
@sec:large-data).
:::

## Paging {#sec:paging}

A table with thousands of rows is a wall, and a wall is not very friendly. The
`pager` option breaks the rows into pages. Give it the page sizes to offer as a
vector, and the first one is used at the start:

```{r}
lt(mtcars[, 1:4]) |> lt_interactive(pager = c(3, 6, Inf), search = FALSE, filter = FALSE)
```

The selector offers 3, 6, or every row (the infinity symbol means all of them).
A size only appears if it would actually split the table, so a short table does
not show a useless pager. Use `pager = FALSE` to show every row with no pager
at all.

Paging works with everything else. Sorting, filtering, and searching are applied
first, and the pager then shows the page of the rows that survived. The row
count beside the pager tells you how many rows the current view holds.

## Filters {#sec:filter}

Search asks one question across the whole table. Filters ask a question about
each column separately, and then keep the rows that pass all of them. Every
column can carry a filter under its header, so the reader can narrow the table
one dimension at a time:

```{r, child = ex('filter')}
```

The first table above asks for `filter = list("auto", Species = FALSE)`. The
`"auto"` picks a filter per column from the data, and the `FALSE` removes the
filter from `Species`. The second table asks for typed controls by name, one
kind of widget per column, and a plain box for every other column.

### Plain boxes

`filter = TRUE` puts a plain box under each header. It matches the same way as
the search, but only in its own column, and it takes the same phrases without
the column name. So under `mpg` you can type `over 25`, and under `cyl` you can
type `is 4 or is 6`.

A plain box suits a reader who knows what to type. Typed widgets suit a reader
who would rather pick from what is there. Use a box when the reader is going to
type, and a widget when the reader is going to pick.

### Let `"auto"` choose

`filter = "auto"` looks at each column and chooses:

-   a **range slider** for numbers, dates, and date-times (or a plain search
    box if every value is the same),
-   a **checklist** for text with at most 10 distinct values,
-   a **plain box** for everything else.

It is the default for `lt_interactive()` because it usually gets the answer
right without asking. Override a single column by naming it in a list:
`list("auto", cyl = "select")` keeps the automatic choice for every column but
`cyl`, which gets a dropdown.

### Typed controls

The typed controls are the widgets behind `"auto"`, and you can ask for any of
them by name:

-   `"select"` is a dropdown of the column's values. It keeps the one value
    chosen.
-   `"checklist"` is a popover of checkboxes. It keeps every value whose box is
    ticked, so the reader can keep several at once. All ticked means no filter.
-   `"range"` is a two-thumb slider for the low and high end. When you do not
    supply the ends, they are read from the data and rounded outwards to values
    that bracket it nicely.

### The funnel, and the expression box

A typed control appears as a little funnel under the column header. Click it to
open a popover with the widget and an expression box side by side. The two stay
in sync: move the slider and the expression updates, or type an expression and
the slider follows. When you type something the widget cannot show, such as a
value outside its choices, the widget hides itself rather than lie about what
it is filtering.

If you want the widget without the expression box, pass a list with
`box = FALSE`, such as `list(type = "select", box = FALSE)`. The reader then
picks from the widget's own choices and nothing else, which is handy for a
strict dropdown.

### Range sliders, by hand and by keyboard

A range slider filters only when you let go. While you drag a thumb, the readout
follows along, but the table waits. Otherwise the rows would reflow under your
cursor and the thumb would jump out from under your finger.

Thumbs also work from the keyboard once they have focus. Arrow keys nudge a thumb
one step at a time, and <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> send it to the
minimum and maximum. Tab to a thumb, and the table is yours.

### Missing values

A `"select"` or `"checklist"` offers `NA` as a choice of its own. Pick it to
keep only the rows where the value is missing, or leave it unticked to set those
rows aside. The filter never hides a missing value by accident.

### Filters on hidden columns

A column you hid with `lt_hide()` has no header to hang a filter on. Instead,
its typed filter moves into the control bar as a labeled chip, showing the
column name and the current value. Click anywhere on the chip to open its
control. This is a good way to offer a filter on a value you do not want to show:

```{r}
lt(mtcars[, 1:5]) |>
  lt_hide(~ mpg) |>
  lt_interactive(
    filter = list(TRUE, mpg = "range", cyl = "checklist"),
    search = FALSE, pager = 5
  )
```

## Row detail {#sec:detail}

Sometimes a row has more to say than fits in a row. The `detail` option adds an
expand caret to each row, and clicking it reveals the rest of that row's story
beneath it. The simplest form names the columns to show, and those can include
columns you hid from the main table:

```{r, child = ex('detail')}
```

For full control, pass a JavaScript function wrapped in `js()`. It receives the
row's raw values, the formatted text, and the row number, and returns a table
spec of its own. Here the detail is a small table that sorts itself:

```{r}
lt(mtcars[, 1:5]) |>
  lt_interactive(
    pager = 3, filter = FALSE, search = FALSE,
    detail = js('(row, i, d) => ({
      data: { field: ["hp", "wt"], value: [d.hp, d.wt] },
      interactive: { sort: ["value"], search: false }
    })')
  )
```

The returned spec is an ordinary table spec, so it can carry its own
`interactive` field. The detail table can be sorted, filtered, or paged, just
like its parent.

## Columns: resizing and hiding {#sec:columns}

### Resizing

Drag the right edge of any header to widen or narrow that column. Widening a
column widens the table and leaves the rest alone. Double-click the edge to fit
the column to its contents, which is the quickest way to rescue a column whose
header is cut short. Starting widths still come from `lt_width()`.

```{r}
lt(head(mtcars[, 1:4])) |> lt_interactive(pager = FALSE, search = FALSE, filter = FALSE) |>
  lt_width(mpg = "8em")
```

Use `resize = FALSE` to fix the widths.

### The column menu {#sec:column-menu}

The `hide` option adds a menu that shows or hides columns. It opens from an eye
button at the start of the search row, and it lists every column by its label.
Uncheck one to hide its header and its cells; check it again to bring it back.

```{r, child = ex('column-menu')}
```

Name columns to start with them hidden, as the example does, or use
`hide = NA` to start with everything visible. Passing `label` swaps the eye icon for a labeled chip in the
control bar, which is clearer when the reader might not know what the eye means.

Older code passes `hide = TRUE` to mean "show the menu". It still works, but it
will be dropped in a future release, so write `hide = NA` for the same effect.

## Profiles: a picture of each column {#sec:profile}

A column's header tells you its name. Its profile tells you its shape. With
`profile = TRUE`, each column header carries a mini chart: a histogram for
numbers and dates, and one bar per category for text. Text with mostly distinct
values gets no chart, because a bar for each name would only be noise.

Hover over a chart to see summary statistics (min, max, and mean for numbers;
the most frequent values for text), along with the count of missing values.
Then filter a column, and the bars light up to show what share of each bucket
your filter kept. It is a surprisingly good way to see what a filter is doing.

```{r, child = ex('profile')}
```

If the headers are already crowded, `profile = "filter"` moves each chart into
its column's filter popover instead. The popover only exists for columns with a
typed filter, so pair this option with `filter = "auto"`:

```{r}
lt(iris) |> lt_interactive(profile = "filter", pager = 3, search = FALSE)
```

## Downloading the view {#sec:download}

The reader has sorted, filtered, and searched their way to exactly the rows they
need. The `download` option turns that view into a file with one click. The
button opens a menu of formats, CSV and RTF (a table for Word, with the title,
column spanners, and notes). The file holds every row the filters and search
keep, in sort order, across all pages, not just the page on screen:

```{r, child = ex('download')}
```

The file uses the displayed text by default, so `4.2` is written as the rounded
figure the reader saw. If you need the underlying numbers at full precision, for
re-importing into analysis code, ask for the raw values instead:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
lt(mtcars) |> lt_interactive(download = list(file = "cars.csv", mode = "raw"))
```

Row detail is never included in the download. Pass `download = TRUE` for a
default file name, or a string to name the file yourself (an extension in it is
replaced by the chosen format's). To offer only some formats, name them: with a
single format the button downloads directly, without a menu.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
lt(mtcars) |> lt_interactive(download = list(file = "cars", formats = "rtf"))
```

## When rows have structure {#sec:structure}

Tables with row groups or indentation carry a shape that sorting could easily
break. **lt** keeps that shape. Sorting and filtering always happen *within* each
group or subtree, never across it, so a group header never gets separated from
its rows, and an indented child never loses its parent.

With separator groups, the groups keep their order, and a group whose rows all
filter out drops its header entirely:

```{r}
d2 = data.frame(
  Region = rep(c("East", "West", "South"), each = 3),
  City = c("NYC", "Boston", "Philly", "LA", "Reno", "Boise", "Austin", "Miami", "Atlanta"),
  Sales = c(42, 17, 23, 55, 9, 14, 31, 48, 26)
)
lt(d2) |> lt_group(~ Region, sep = TRUE) |> lt_interactive(pager = 5)
```

With rowspan groups, clicking a group header reorders whole blocks, and with
several group columns the view stays nested, so an inner column only reorders
within its parent. The spanning cells are redrawn to match.

Indentation sorts siblings under each parent and carries each subtree along.
Filtering a deep child keeps its ancestors visible, so the reader can always see
where a row belongs:

```{r}
d3 = data.frame(
  Item = c("Fruit", "Apple", "Pear", "Berry", "Grain", "Rice", "Oat", "Wheat"),
  Qty = c(0, 12, 7, 5, 0, 30, 8, 19)
)
lt(d3) |> lt_indent(c(2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8), level = 1) |> lt_interactive(pager = 5)
```

Spanners, styles, and footnotes are no obstacle to any of this.

## Long tables in a scrolling box {#sec:scroll-box}

Sometimes you do not want a page scrollbar at all. Put the table in a box with a
fixed height instead, and the table scrolls inside it. With `lt_wrap()`, you can
set that box's style directly. The header is sticky, so the column names,
spanners, and controls stay in view however far the reader scrolls:

```{r}
lt(mtcars[, 1:4]) |>
  lt_interactive(pager = FALSE, filter = FALSE) |>
  lt_wrap(style = "max-height: 14em; overflow-y: auto")
```

Printing an interactive table in the viewer or a browser already fits it to the
window in the same way, so a tall table scrolls inside its frame rather than
pushing the page around.

## The data viewer {#sec:viewer}

Most of the time, the table you want is the one that answers "what is in this
data frame?". `lt_viewer()` is that table, ready made. It is a shorthand for
`lt_interactive()` with a few sensible defaults: each column shows its type and
a profile, the column menu is on, and the title is the expression you passed:

```{r, child = ex('viewer')}
```

Printed at the console, a viewer opens in the RStudio or Positron pane when it is
available, or in your browser otherwise. Remove the title with
`lt_header(NULL)`. Every argument of `lt_interactive()` also works here, so
`lt_viewer(iris, pager = 5)` is a viewer with five-row pages.

Use `lt_viewer()` to explore, and `lt_interactive()` to publish. The viewer
packs in types and profiles for the explorer's benefit. In a report, a leaner
table that says exactly what you mean usually reads better.

## Large data: serving rows from R {#sec:large-data}

Everything so far keeps the rows in the browser. That is fine for thousands of
rows, and it starts to hurt somewhere past a hundred thousand. For data of
millions of rows, `lt_serve()` keeps the rows in R instead. The browser asks for
only the page it is showing, and each time the reader sorts, filters, searches,
or turns the page, R sends back just those rows.

```{r, child = ex('serve')}
```

The app is local, built on `xfun::new_app()`, so it lives in your R session and
serves the table while that session runs. In a Shiny app, you do not need it at
all: return the table from `render_lt()`, and the session serves the rows.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
output$big = lt_interactive(my_data) |> lt_serve() |> render_lt()
```

There is a price for the extra reach, and it is worth knowing before you lean on
it:

-   **Expressions run in R.** Filter and search expressions such as `x > 5` or
    `x != "A"` must be valid R. The phrases and the widgets' own filters work
    in both places, and a missing value never passes an expression unless the
    expression is negated.
-   **Substring matching uses the underlying values.** Search and text filters
    look at the raw values rather than the formatted text, so a number is
    matched as its full precision, not as the rounded figure on screen.
-   **Profiles and choices come from all the data.** They are computed once when
    the app starts, so a dropdown lists every value, not just the current page.
    Plots drawn in cells scale to the current page.
-   **Some table features are missing.** Row groups, indentation, row-specific
    styles and footnotes, and external filter predicates do not work through
    the server. A JavaScript row detail sees only the current page.
-   **The download fetches every row of the view.** It is complete, but a
    huge view takes a while to arrive.

::: {.callout-warning data-legend="For viewing, not publishing"}
A local app is for looking at a table from your own R session: the console, RStudio,
a remote session, or a notebook. It is not for publishing. A static document
(R Markdown, Quarto, litedown) has no R session behind it once it is rendered,
and webR or shinylive cannot run the app at all. For a published page, use
`lt_interactive()` with the rows in the page, or bring your own server.
:::

### Bringing your own server

When the rows live somewhere else, such as a database or a folder of Parquet
files, give `lt_serve()` a `url` instead. Your server answers the browser's
requests with JSON pages, and the table only needs to name its columns. A
zero-row data frame is enough, because the first page is fetched too:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
lt(data.frame(id = integer(), x = numeric())) |>
  lt_interactive() |>
  lt_serve(url = "https://example.org/rows")
```

The request and response format is the same protocol the JavaScript runtime
speaks, and it is described in full in @sec:server, in the JavaScript chapter
(@chp:js). Any server that follows it can power a table, whatever it is built
on.
